rv.q: It’s an oddity, this, but worth seeing for him.
While the two lead performances compel, its glaring deficit is that it strains too hard to jazz things up experimentally.
The first half is pulled down by the weight of its laboured reinvention.
Sadly, Anthony Lau’s febrile expressionist production is so overheated that it’s impossible to ignore the implausibilities in the storyline.
It also liberates star Ben Daniels from period constraints, freeing him up to deliver what is easily the best stage performance of the year to date.

Most critics praise Lau for taking a bold approach to dusty and unloved Rattigan play, but for some, the arch inventiveness goes too far, getting in the way of a story about corruption that could speak to us more sincerely and directly.
The strange carapace works for the seedy and sinister first half, which is essentially a tense race against time.
These witty touches are refreshing – but they feel like a bit of a mismatch with Rattigan’s serious portrait of moral corruption, which offers more to respect than to enjoy.
When some of the unnecessary artifice is stripped away, however, this is an astutely written drama the National were right to revisit.
Rattigan's MAN AND BOY isn't considered among his finest plays.
Nonetheless, Daniels continues to hold the attention, adeptly shifting his physicality from strength to frailty.
